From scattered churn signals to a shared retention workflow

Connecting AI-detected signals, account-manager context, and a shared view of churn risk.

Overview

Competitor and churn signals from client calls were scattered across Google Chat and personal spreadsheets, leaving gaps in the information available for retention planning.

I designed a connected workflow: AI flags mentions, n8n prepares a HubSpot questionnaire, and account managers have three days to review it before submission. A daily dashboard sync gives stakeholders a shared view while distinguishing reviewed records from automatic submissions.

Key Impact

83% reported increase in response rate

An increase in the existing churn-risk response rate, reported from the project. Automated collection and daily shared reporting gave retention stakeholders a centralized basis for action.

The problem

A signal could be recorded—and still disappear.

Gong recorded client calls, but competitor and churn mentions reached retention decision-makers only when an account manager passed them on. Updates arrived through Google Chat and personal spreadsheets, leaving stakeholders without a shared view of what had been heard or needed attention. Important signals could slip through the cracks or reach the right people too late to act.

How might we capture important churn signals and make them accessible to the right stakeholders in time for informed retention decisions?

Research insights

Manual reporting was the bottleneck.

I interviewed 6+ team leads to understand where the competitive-intelligence process broke down. Account managers had limited time for manual reporting, and flagging potential churn was not consistently prioritized. Team leads received scattered updates across disconnected channels, sometimes too late to plan a response.

Across UX/UI, research, automation, and CRM integration, I focused on reducing that reporting burden: capture signals early, sync them automatically to a shared dashboard, and give account managers an easy way to review the information and add context.

Research insights → design direction
What was happeningWhat the design needed to do
Manual reporting competed with account managers’ other priorities.Prepare the record automatically, so managers can review and enrich it instead of starting from scratch.
Signals arrived across Google Chat and personal spreadsheets.Sync signals daily to one dashboard accessible to all relevant stakeholders.
In the manual process, a form cannot submit without account-manager input.Give managers three days to validate and add context. Then automatically submit unactioned records, keeping review status visible so stakeholders can distinguish them from reviewed information.

Workflow design

Automate the handoff. Keep human review explicit.

The workflow links detection to a prepared questionnaire, gives the relevant account manager three days to review, and syncs the collected information daily. Automatic submission keeps information moving, helping decision makers form a retention plan in time.

UX Design

Two paths to a shared view of churn risk.

I designed the final flow around two audiences: account managers who supply relationship context, and decision makers who need a timely view of client risk. Prefilled records keep manual input focused on validation and additional context, helping signals reach the people planning a retention response with less effort from account managers.

The queue makes reviews easy to find; the dashboard connects account-level detail with portfolio and competitor patterns. Managers can revisit submitted information to add context as the client relationship evolves.

Final solution

Trace a risk pattern back to its source.

The overview shows trends and priority accounts. Intelligence search and filters narrow the investigation by competitor, risk, manager, or review status; account details keep the excerpt and review history close. Stakeholders can inspect the context behind a signal instead of relying on an aggregate alone.

The impact

More signals reached a shared starting point.

BeforeManual reporting across separate channels
→
AfterAutomated collection with daily shared visibility

The project reported an 83% increase in the existing churn-risk response rate. Broader collection and centralized access supported retention planning. This is a reported rate increase, not a claim of 83% less response time or independently validated lift.

What the evidence does—and does not—show

Raw timings, denominator, and calculation are unavailable. The public prototype’s account counts, revenue exposure, and risk scores are fictional examples, not business outcomes. No retained-revenue figure is claimed.

Reflections

Two lessons I’ll take forward.

The best UX improvements aren't always new interfaces.

This project challenged me to think beyond screens and interactions. The core problem wasn't a poorly designed interface, but a fragmented process across multiple tools. I learned that meaningful UX improvements sometimes come from redesigning the underlying workflow rather than introducing another standalone product.

Automation should reduce effort, not eliminate human judgment.

Automating competitive intelligence taught me the importance of balancing efficiency with trust. While AI helped identify and capture signals at scale, preserving human validation ensured that insights remained reliable and actionable. I learned to design systems that use automation without losing the contextual understanding people bring to decision-making.
